body_markdown:
In 1989, the boutique German car manufacturer RUF released a 20-minute movie to promote a 200-mph version of the Porsche 911 Turbo called the CTR. The car world knew the machine by its nickname: Yellowbird.


The film, called *Faszination on the Nürburgring* , was the first of its kind, showcasing driver Stefan Roser[hooning the Yellowbird around Germany’s racetrack](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3U26ddkVw2Q) . Most of the shots are what’s called point-of-view angle, so the viewer feels like they’re behind the wheel as Roser drifts the car through every corner. Ruf and Roser’s influence can be seen in Ken Block videos, the golden era of *Top Gear,* and even the slidefests on Hagerty’s own[YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/hagerty) .


Since RUF’s film came out before the internet, it went viral primarily via word of mouth and VHS tapes. I didn’t get my hands on a grainy copy until many years after its introduction. I must have watched it 10 times straight. There on the screen was seemingly everything I loved about cars: the speed, the danger, the aggression one could apply behind the wheel. I’ve never forgotten it.


That emotional connection between movies and cars is the reason we dedicated an entire issue of *Hagerty Drivers Club* magazine to the topic. We’re now posting the material on our website, and you can view it all[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .


Just like the directors who make those movies, we had a hard time deciding what to include in this issue and what to leave on the cutting room floor.


At first, we couldn’t even agree on what counted as a car movie. Is a documentary about another car movie itself a car movie? I decided it was and wrote about[Steve McQueen, The Man & Le Mans.](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3504604/) Stay tuned to[Hagerty.com/media](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) to check it out.


What about McQueen’s famous flick, *Bullitt* ? “Not a car movie!” declared editor-at-large Aaron Robinson. Before you get out your pitchforks,[read his always thoughtful rationale](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/why-bullitt-isnt-a-car-movie/) . Note that our own CEO, McKeel Hagerty, wasn’t quite convinced—he shares why[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/mckeel-the-cars-and-car-movies-that-move-me/) .


We wound up compiling a list of our editors’ personal favorite car movies. You’ll surely recognize many. A few might surprise you (Hint: One is French). Think we left out a clear winner? After you’ve[read the list](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/11-of-the-best-car-movies-according-to-us/) , feel free to comment below and tell us why.


That’s the fun and the madness of a topic like the one we’ve tackled here. There are no wrong answers. What’s certain is that cars often make movies better and that the right movie, like *Faszination* , stirs and enhances our own love for cars.


RUF Automobile GmbH


Thanks to modern technology, it’s never been easier to make movies. Phones now film in high definition, and with a few easy techniques, you can be your own Steven Spielberg. To help you get started, we’ve included tips from our resident short-form video expert, Isaac Shapiro. I’ve experimented myself: You can view my first attempts on Instagram[@lwebster19](https://www.instagram.com/lwebster19) . We hope you enjoy the series,[which you can follow here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) —then get out there on your own and add to your car story.


*This story first appeared in the “Movies and Cars” digital issue of* Hagerty Drivers Club *magazine.[Join the club](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine/) to receive our award-winning magazine and enjoy insider access to automotive events, discounts, roadside assistance, and more.*
